description: We are a team of software engineering students from the National University “Kyiv Aviation Institute,” bringing a strong blend of full-stack development and hardware expertise to the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Building on our momentum from the 2025 Kyiv event, our team specializes in crafting scalable architectures, real-time data processing, and modern applications.
summary: Hold On, Mars! is a first-person co-op Roblox game for kids aged 7–12. The players are the crew of a Mars base. Together they keep water, food and oxygen running until the launch window opens on sol 5 and the rocket can take them home. If they miss it, the crew has to hold on longer. Each sol teaches one real limit of living on Mars: building an ice drill from metals found in rocks, cleaning dusty solar panels, digging ice where NASA's ice map shows it, sheltering from a solar storm taken from a real NASA DONKI flare, and fixing machines that break. Mission Control answers through Sparky, the base's radio rover, with today's real Earth–Mars signal delay from NASA JPL Horizons. Every choice costs time, water or safety. If the crew runs out, nobody gets hurt: the mission stops, the game explains what went wrong, and the crew can try again.
details:
Hold On, Mars! is a first-person co-op survival game on Roblox. It is designed for ages 7–12, but anyone can play. The players are the crew of a Mars base, not spectators. The game is cross-platform, so friends can play together on different devices. The mission lasts five sols (Martian days). Each sol has a short briefing from Earth, two or three crew objectives and one real lesson about living on Mars:


- Sol 1, Landing. Everything we need must be found on Mars. Put on a space suit, go outside, collect rock samples and sort them into iron, nickel and manganese.
- Sol 2, Dust and power. Dust blocks sunlight and plants grow slowly. Clean the dusty solar panels after a dust storm, fix the water pump by soldering its circuit board, plant crops.
- Sol 3, Water from ice. Water is hidden as ice under the ground. Build an ice drill from the metals, dig ice where NASA's ice map shows it, take shelter from a solar storm.
- Sol 4, Things break. Machines fail and repairs cost time. Repair the radar after a marsquake, fix the oxygen generator, harvest crops.
- Sol 5, The launch window. Planets must line up to fly home. Tell Earth the crew is ready, collect 10 rock samples in total over the mission (plain rocks, hematite, iron meteorites and manganese rocks) to take home to Earth, launch the rocket.

If the crew misses the launch window, the game goes on and they have to hold on longer.


How it works

- Three shared resources: water, food and oxygen. The crew drinks and eats every sol. Ice gives water, the greenhouse turns water into food, the base needs air.
- No free choices. Planting costs water. Hiding from a storm costs work time. Working through it builds up radiation dose. Emergency supplies from Earth cost four game hours.
- Radiation dose is a personal meter. It grows at the real Mars surface rate measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument and rises sharply during a solar storm. It shows the dose as "days of Mars background", which is easy to understand.
- Events from real data: the solar storm uses a real flare from NASA DONKI; the dust storm is the 2018 global dust storm seen by Curiosity REMS; a cold-night card uses recent REMS temperatures; a CME warning uses the DONKI WSA-ENLIL forecast for Mars. Every card shows the source, the real date and a LIVE or ARCHIVED label.
- Sparky, the radio rover, is the crew's link to Mission Control. Players type a question or press a quick button. The answer comes back after today's real round-trip light time from Earth to Mars, fetched from NASA JPL Horizons when the server starts (about 11 minutes each way today, sped up like the game clock). During solar conjunction, Sparky has no signal.
- Greenhouse with six crops NASA really grew in space (radish, dwarf wheat, red lettuce, mizuna mustard, dwarf tomato, chili pepper). Each one grows at a speed based on how many days it took on the ISS.
- Ice map at the science station: NASA's "Treasure Map for Water Ice on Mars" (2019), with the colour legend explained.
- Soft failure. If the base runs out of air, or the whole crew runs out of water or food, the mission stops. A debrief explains what went wrong, and the crew chooses "Earth sends supplies" or "Start again". No death or scary scenes.


Benefits

- Players learn real constraints by playing them: why ice depth matters, why dust is a problem for solar power, why you cannot call Earth and get an instant answer.
- Co-op play turns survival into teamwork: one player drills, another fixes the pump, another tends the greenhouse.
- Failing is safe and short, so players try again and learn from the debrief.
- Real NASA data makes the game different each time and connects it to what is happening in space now.

What we hope to achieve

A game that a class or a group of friends can play in one session and come away knowing what it really takes to live on Mars. Next steps: a longer campaign (repairs, new storms, rescue), saved progress, and more live data.

Tools and technology

- Roblox Studio and Luau. The server owns all game state; clients only show it.
- Rojo to keep code in Git and sync it into Studio, Wally for packages, Selene (lint), StyLua (format), Lune for headless tests of the mission rules and game math.
- HttpService on the server for NASA APIs (DONKI, JPL Horizons), one request at start with a saved snapshot as fallback.
- Roblox TextGenerator for Mission Control's answers, with TextService chat filtering, an off-topic check and a rule that any number in the answer must come from our checked fact list.
- Node.js scripts to download and save NASA data snapshots; Git and GitHub for teamwork.
